newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi slams budget, Italy shopkeepers protest.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi slams budget, Italy shopkeepers protest.

text.p: Italian opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi attacked the government on Monday for steamrolling through its tough 1997 budget as shopkeepers across the country protested against planned increases in taxes.
"I'm worried not just for the 1997 budget but for the whole country. Government parties are occupying all the posts of power, we're seeing a hegemony being created," Berlusconi said.
The leader of the centre-right Freedom Alliance was speaking to reporters while attending a Milan demonstration organised by Italy's retailers' association Confcommercio.

Dubbed "Tax Day Two", shopkeepers throughout Italy closed their shops and took to the streets in condemnation of what they called a new fiscal "hammering" with higher taxes planned in centre-left Prime Minister Romano Prodi's austerity budget.
The first Tax Day was in March when shopkeepers pulled down their shutters in protest over high taxes, a central issue in April's general election which brought Prodi to power.
Tax rates in Italy are among the highest in western Europe and the country has some of the most complicated payment rules.

Prodi at the weekend defended his controversial budget and said he was sure parliament would approve the measures aiming to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) from Italy's projected deficit and bring the country close to European monetary union.
Berlusconi accused the government of steamrolling the budget law through parliament which has to pass it by December 31.
"The government is preventing the opposition from putting forward proposals," he said.

Asked if he thought the government intended to force the measures through parliament by resorting to confidence votes, a measure aimed to sweep aside amendments and filibustering, Berlusconi said, "I am sure of it."
By using confidence votes the government "is preventing us from making suggestions and from supervising in parliament the action of the government," he said.
"This is an ideological and distructive budget, whereas in our counter-programme all the needs and desires of tradesmen are addressed," Berlusconi added.
Shopkeepers in 200 major Italian cities displayed posters in their windows saying "Closed for mourning due to the budget."
A demonstration in Milan began with a minute's silence in memory, the retailers body said, of the 200,000 shops forced to close between 1992 and 1995 by tough economic conditions.
Confcommercio said shops taking part in the protest would keep their lights on throughout the night with the motto "Let's give light to the market."
Confcommercio chairman Sergio Bille told reporters the protest was basically against the increase of an already crippling tax burden.

"We need to change the mechanism of public spending, give more tax breaks for investment and relaunch domestic demand," he said, adding the government should make clear details of the 12 trillion lire "Tax for Europe" contained in the 1997 budget, expected to hit every taxpayer in the country by a hike in income tax.
Prodi's budget, which is weighted heavily with new revenue-raising schemes, has also been criticised by employers' federations for largely avoiding a structural overhaul of welfare spending.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio also stepped into the fray last week, saying the government should concentrate its efforts on structural spending cuts.
